what_its_for: Dapsone is an antibiotic and anti-inflammatory medicine. It is mainly used to treat leprosy (a bacterial skin infection) and a skin condition called dermatitis herpetiformis (a blistering, itchy rash). Your doctor may also prescribe it to prevent or treat a type of pneumonia called Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), especially in people with weakened immune systems.
how_to_take: Take dapsone tablets by mouth, usually once a day or as directed by your doctor. You may take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help reduce stomach upset. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Do not stop taking dapsone without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better, because stopping early may allow the infection or condition to return.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition, weight, and other health factors. Common doses are: For leprosy: adults often start at 50 mg to 100 mg once daily. For dermatitis herpetiformis: adults usually start at 50 mg once daily, and the dose may be slowly increased up to 300 mg per day based on how you respond. For PCP prevention: adults typically take 100 mg once daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Do not change your dose without asking your doctor.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store dapsone tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them in a dry place, away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store them in the bathroom. Keep dapsone and all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use dapsone after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of unused or expired medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking dapsone, as it may increase the risk of liver problems and side effects. Avoid taking antacids that contain magnesium trisilicate, as they can reduce how well dapsone works. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking any other medicines, vitamins, or supplements, especially rifampin, trimethoprim, folic acid inhibitors, or blood thinners, as these may interact with dapsone. Avoid prolonged sun exposure, as dapsone may make your skin more sensitive to sunlight. Use sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following: yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, or severe stomach pain (possible signs of liver problems); bluish or grayish color of the lips, fingernails, or skin; unusual tiredness, shortness of breath, or rapid heartbeat (possible signs of low red blood cell counts such as methemoglobinemia or hemolytic anemia); severe skin rash, blistering, peeling, or sores in the mouth (possible signs of a serious allergic reaction); fever, swollen lymph nodes, or flu-like symptoms that do not go away; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face, lips, throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Dapsone may take several weeks to months before you see full improvement, depending on your condition. For skin conditions like dermatitis herpetiformis, you may start to notice less itching and fewer blisters within a few weeks, but it can take longer for the rash to fully clear. For leprosy, treatment can last for months to years. Do not stop taking the medicine just because you feel better. Follow your doctor's instructions for the full length of treatment.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Dapsone should only be used during pregnancy if the benefit clearly outweighs the risk. It may cause blood problems in newborns if taken near the time of delivery. Breastfeeding: Dapsone passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding while on this medicine. Children: Dapsone can be used in children under careful medical supervision, with doses adjusted based on weight and condition. Elderly: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects, especially blood-related problems. Regular blood tests may be needed. G6PD Deficiency: People with a genetic condition called G6PD deficiency are at much higher risk of serious red blood cell problems (hemolytic anemia) with dapsone. Tell your doctor if you have this condition before starting dapsone. Kidney or Liver Disease: If you have kidney or liver problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely.
